extracted.intended_audience: railway engineers, railway company managers, and general readers interested in 19th-century railway practice and safety
extracted.subtask_description: Practical standards, safety recommendations, economic and professional practices advocated or exemplified by George Stephenson for railway construction, locomotive design, train operation, and personnel selection in the early railway era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self‑acting carriage brakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a system of self‑acting brakes on every carriage to increase safety; brakes should be thrown into action by the momentum of the running train immediately when the moving power is checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stephenson's plan: use train momentum to apply brakes automatically when engine power is reduced; brakes to be controllable by the guard via a connecting line running along the train so they can be thrown out of gear when necessary. He considered this the most important arrangement for increasing railway safety and even advocated legislative enforcement. Claimed effect: 'if self-acting brakes were put upon every carriage, scarcely any accident could take place.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Self‑acting signals worked by locomotives
rubrics_metrics.description: Signals of the line should be self-acting and be operated by locomotives as they pass along the railway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an additional safety measure alongside self‑acting brakes; recommended to be adopted for public safety and, ideally, enforced by law. No detailed mechanical design here, but presented as a complement to automated braking to reduce accidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed limits tied to line conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit speeds: recommend no railway ought to exceed 40 miles an hour on the most favourable gradient; on curved lines the speed ought not to exceed 24 or 25 miles an hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stephenson argued high velocity creates danger and increased wear; although higher speeds might be technically possible, they are often unnecessary and increase risk and expense. He acknowledged engines could be built for higher speeds but warned of material limits and fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design tradeoff: speed versus strength and cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Every increase of speed increases strain on rails and rolling stock, requiring heavier engines, better-fastened rails, and higher working expenses; iron 'tires' and rails fatigue and may break at flaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for design: do not increase speed beyond what the quality of rails and rolling stock can safely support. Stephenson emphasized knowing 'where to stop' mechanically—a pound will weigh a pound—and cautioned about contracted, poor-quality rails ('little better than cast metal').

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate goods/mineral traffic from passenger traffic
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mix heavy merchandise and coal trains with passenger trains; construct railways exclusively devoted to goods/mineral traffic if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: passenger trains require higher speeds and force other trains to run faster, increasing wear and costs. For profitable mineral transport, run long coal trains at low speeds on less perfect, less expensive lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low‑speed coal trains as economic policy
rubrics_metrics.description: A succession of long coal trains run at from ten to fourteen miles an hour would pay very well; coal and most goods can wait while passengers cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stephenson cites Stockton and Darlington Company experience: larger profit when running coal at low speeds (example pricing: halfpenny a ton per mile) than after introduction of fast passenger trains which increased working expenses and reduced margins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept lower construction standards for slow goods lines
rubrics_metrics.description: For coal/mineral traffic run at low speeds, a less perfect road and less expensive works will do well enough; directness is less important if the line is flat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance for route planning and cost control: prioritize utility and cheapness for freight lines; avoid overbuilding for speed when unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit high velocity in public interest despite technical possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Although locomotives might be made to travel very high speeds (Stephenson notes theoretical possibilities up to 100 mph), the governing criterion should be what speed best suits the public—not merely what is technically possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a normative guideline balancing innovation with public safety, economy, and material limits. Speed should not be pursued for its own sake because it multiplies expense and risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard control and centralised actuation for safety devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Safety devices (brakes) should be under the control of a guard via a connecting line running the length of the train to permit manual overriding or release when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines automatic actuation with human supervision: automatic brakes thrown into action by momentum but controllable by guard to ensure operational flexibility and incident management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select and promote assistants by observed character and talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose young men best fitted to carry out plans by intuitive knowledge of character; encourage and promote those showing zeal, diligence, and integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stephenson emphasised practical selection over pedigree: he identified promising youths from among workers (carpenter, industrious by-hours worker) and gave them training and positions, crediting many engineers' rise to such encouragement. This is guidance for personnel recruitment and mentorship in an engineering shop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional billing practice and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: When preparing accounts for multiple companies, charge fairly—Stephenson initially directed charging time proportionally at ten guineas a day, but (after counsel) charged an entire day's fee to each company while reducing the daily amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates a professional norm balancing simplicity, customary practice, and fairness to clients: professional fees should be consistent with industry practice and adjusted to reflect reasonable rates; also shows reluctance to profiteer and a tendency to reduce rates to conform to norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate perseverance and self‑education
rubrics_metrics.description: Persevere in self-improvement: Stephenson used public addresses (Mechanics' Institutes) to exhort working men to persevere in acquiring knowledge, using his life as an example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as social and moral guidance for aspiring mechanics and engineers—personal perseverance and education are key to advancement and success.
